claims.text: Nanoscale chemical heterogeneities in HfNbTaTiZr create regions with different thermal expansion coefficients.
Thermal-expansion mismatch between heterogeneous regions generates internal residual stresses.
Mismatch-induced residual stresses alter dislocation mobility and elastic properties over a wide temperature range.
Conventionally processed HfNbTaTiZr is a single-phase alloy.
Conventionally processed HfNbTaTiZr may contain minor nanoscale chemical clustering or segregation.
Rapid quenching will maintain a homogenized HfNbTaTiZr microstructure with minimal heterogeneity.
Controlled aging or annealing will promote nanoscale clusters with thermal-expansion characteristics distinct from the matrix.
Precipitate evolution is expected in the 600–800 °C aging regime.
Nanoscale clusters or precipitates in HfNbTaTiZr possess a thermal expansion coefficient different from that of the matrix.
Heating and cooling induce localized residual-stress fields through differential expansion of clusters and matrix.
The residual stresses modify dislocation motion and thereby affect tensile creep and work hardening.
The residual stresses modify the temperature dependence of the elastic moduli.
Compared with homogenized samples, samples with enhanced nanoscale heterogeneity will have altered tensile creep rates near 1250 °C.
Residual-stress-induced strain hardening may lower the creep rate at a given applied stress.
Enhanced nanoscale heterogeneity will modify the microhardness response following cold rolling.
Enhanced nanoscale heterogeneity may reduce the temperature dependence of elastic moduli or produce a modulus plateau between 293 and 1100 K.
A homogenized, rapidly quenched baseline will lack significant internal stresses caused by thermal-expansion mismatch.
The proposed mechanism will be most pronounced from 600 to 1250 °C.
The proposed mechanism may be negligible at low thermal driving force or when the alloy remains fully homogenized.
